newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Volvo sells Renault stake for $740 million.
newsitem.headline: Volvo sells Renault stake for $740 million.

text.p: Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo said Thursday it sold its remaining stake in French automaker Renault to the Union Bank of Switzerland for 5.9 billion crowns ($740 million).
The stake, amounting to 11.38 percent of Renault's capital, was left over from a failed merger of the automakers in 1993.
Volvo said it will have a capital gain of 750 million crowns ($94.5 million) from the sale.
"This seemed a good time to sell," said BZW analyst Andy Blair-Smith.

"Volvo now has this money to plough back into new model development, expand truck operations in Eastern Europe, and to look for acquisitions in the U.S. truck market where Volvo is a potential bridegroom for Renault's Mack division."
"The company can now look for potential acquisition targets in its truck and construction equipment sectors," said Lars Glemstedt of Aros Securities.

Volvo has pursued a divestment programme since early 1994, when then-chief executive Soren Gyll began to strip down the seafood-to-stockbroking empire built up by his predecessor Pehr Gyllenhammar to concentrate on its core automotive businesses.
"The sale of our stake in Renault is fully in line with the strategy the board decided on at the start of 1994," Volvo Chief Executive Leif Johansson said in a statement.
Meanwhile, in Paris Renault said it was not surprised by Volvo's sale of the Renault stake and would similarly shed its 3 percent Volvo holding when the time was right.
"When we judge that it would be a good moment to sell the stake, we will sell it," said a spokeswoman for the French company.
Volvo's sale of the Renault stake leaves it with just one major shareholding to dispose of -- a stake of about 4 percent in troubled U.S./Swedish drugs company Pharmacia & Upjohn.
"It's not on the cards right now (to sell P&U shares)," Volvo spokesman Stefan Karlsson told Reuters.
Volvo sold two-thirds of its 14 percent P&U holding last summer, but Volvo spokesman Stefan Karlsson said there would be no more major disposals for the time being.
Major spin-offs to date have included Swedish Match, which was paid out as a bonus dividend to Volvo shareholders in early 1996, and the Finnish food group Cultor.
